paras: The forced levee labor at Newport, Arkansas, was the reported compulsion of Black men, at the point of shotguns, to work on the town's flooding levees on the night of August 22-23 and the morning of August 23, 1915. According to one wire version, armed white citizens threatened the workers with death if they relaxed. No one was reported hurt, and the claim reached papers from Arizona to Wisconsin as a line in flood news.

In late August 1915 the White River rose higher than it had in fifteen years, flooding thousands of acres of bottomland. At Newport the river came over the Rock Island levee, a new $25,000 causeway over Newport Lake broke, and business, water and electric service were suspended. Steamers were taking families out of the bottoms, some of them from trees.

On the night of August 22, virtually every man and boy in Newport answered a call for volunteers to work on the caving levee. Black men "were forced to join," and about 200 men worked until 4 a.m., when the levee broke in half a dozen places. By the morning of August 23, according to an Associated Press dispatch from Little Rock, hundreds of volunteers were on the levee and Black men "had been forced at the point of shotguns to join them."

A second version, credited to "telegraphic advices" reaching Little Rock, said the whole population and farmers for miles around were repairing six breaks in the levee. In that account white citizens stood guard with shotguns, "compelling negro farm hands to keep at work, threatening them with death if they relaxed." Arkansas papers added that Judge M. M. Stuckey of Newport headed a gang of forty men working on the levee, but did not connect him to the guards.
No report of an arrest, inquiry or denial appears in the coverage, and none of the workers or guards was named.

The white press carried the episode only as a sentence inside flood dispatches led by inundation, drownings and crop damage. The Associated Press version ran the same day in the Topeka State Journal, the Nogales Daily Herald and the Medford Mail Tribune, and the next day in the Omaha Daily Bee, which tucked it into a Missouri flood story. A few editors lifted it into headlines: the Topeka paper ran "Negroes Forced at Point of Gun to Join Them," and the weekly Tabor Independent in South Dakota printed "Negroes Forced at Point of Shotguns to Labor on Levee Reinforcement."

The southern dailies that carried a shorter Associated Press text, the Montgomery Advertiser and the Pensacola Journal, hedged the claim: Black men, "it is said," had been forced to join, with no mention of guns. The death-threat version appeared in the Beatrice Daily Express and, two days later, in the weekly River Falls Journal in Wisconsin. In Arkansas, three weeklies, the Nevada County Picayune, the Ozark Spectator and the Pulaskian, printed a Newport report with the shotgun line on August 27, without comment.
None of the papers questioned the practice or called it lawless; the forced labor appeared alongside rescues and stock roaming the streets as part of the town's fight against the water.

reader.title: Forced levee labor at Newport, Arkansas (1915)
bases: Black men were reportedly compelled at shotgun point, under threat of death, to work on the Newport levee during a flood (A1, A8, A12); it was impressed emergency labor, not debt servitude.

Two differently worded wire versions from Little Rock (A1, A2 and A8, A10) and an Arkansas report under a Newport dateline (A12, A13) agree on forced labor at gunpoint, though all relay unattributed 'reports', one hedges with 'it is said' (A6), and none names a witness.

framing.detail: Most papers carried the forced labor as one sentence in flood news headed by the inundation, drownings and crop losses, without comment.
The Topeka State Journal and the Tabor Independent made it a subhead: 'Negroes Forced at Point of Gun to Join Them' and 'Negroes Forced at Point of Shotguns to Labor on Levee Reinforcement'.
The Montgomery Advertiser's version hedged the claim with 'it is said' and dropped the shotguns.
